data.title: Oil prices up after new strikes on Saudi infrastructure
data.description:
Oil prices on Monday leaped more than 4 percent after Yemen-based militant Houthis struck Saudi Arabia’s infrastructure and ships, leaving one crucial pipeline out of service for weeks.

The global benchmark for crude oil, Brent crude, settled at $105.66 per barrel as of Monday afternoon. West Texas Intermediate (WTI), the benchmark in the U.S., rose to $101.28.

The average price of gas in the U.S. reached $4.32, a 7-cent increase since last week, and the average price for diesel reached $6.23, a new record, both according to data from AAA.

Saudi Arabia’s 745-mile-long East-West Pipeline has helped the government move crude production from the Persian Gulf ports to the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea, where tankers can export oil.

Saudi officials familiar with the Thursday attack on the pipeline told the Associated Press that it could take 3-5 weeks to repair, though it could partially work while crews work to fix it. The pipeline moved a weekly average of 2.6 million to 4 million barrels a day since late August.

The Norway-based energy analyst Rystad Energy said Monday that the increase in the price of Brent crude “is a clear signal that the market is increasingly pricing in a significant loss of supply.”

The Houthis, a proxy of the Iranian regime, entered the U.S.-Israeli conflict in Iran to retaliate against Gulf state attacks on Iran after calling on Persian Gulf countries, the U.S. and Israel to seek a path to diplomacy and peace with Iran. They warned that they would retaliate if the conflict escalated.

The Houthis also captured the crucial islands of Greater and Lesser Hanish, which are both located 100 miles north of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to Saudi Arabia’s key Asian markets. The islands are also 20 miles from a U.S. military base in Djibouti in the Horn of Africa.

The rebels also took over the port city of Mokha, another Red Sea port crucial to shipping, risking opening up a new front in the Iran war. The Saudis have reportedly urged President Trump to launch strikes on the Houthis, while the U.S. has sent more than 100 advisors to help the Saudis in their fight with the rebel forces.

Oil exports through the Red Sea after passing through the East-West Pipeline have been an alternative to exporting oil out of the Strait of Hormuz. The Iranian regime has effectively cut off the transit of oil out of the region in response to U.S. strikes, causing gas and oil prices to skyrocket.

Diesel prices have soared to record highs as Ukraine carries out its drone strikes on Russian refineries. Trump urged Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to call off further attacks on these refineries.

“He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia,” Trump told reporters on Sunday. We spoke to Mr. Zelenskyy about it. There are plenty of other targets. Don’t hit diesel fuel, because that’s hurting the world.”

data.title: Thune: Legislation to regulate AI needs to have a 'light touch'
data.description:
Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) on Monday said any legislation Congress passes to regulate AI must have a “light touch” so as not to stifle innovation and tempered recent warnings that superintelligent AI could exterminate humanity as a “worst-case scenario.”

“It needs to strike a balance, light touch. You don’t want to stifle innovation but you also want to make sure that the more advanced threats can be mitigated,” he told reporters.

“Obviously there’s a responsibility for the companies to do that when it comes to the frontier on some of these models,” he added. “There is a way in which Congress can put guardrails around those types of more consequential threats without in any way harming our ability to stay ahead in the AI race, which I also think is very important.”

Thune made his comments after Jacob Coxon, a former researcher for OpenAI and Anthropic, warned that neither company is acting responsibility and are “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.”

This has fueled fears that superintelligent AI could turn against humanity with devastating consequences, something that Thune on Monday downplayed as a “worst-case scenario.”

“I think there are some of these frontier models … I think there are some potential consequential risks associated with AI. But there are always people who are creating a worst-case-scenario-type conversation out there and I think that you have to try, like all things, figure out what the realistic approach ought to be,” he said.

“Put guardrails around it, like I said, I think on some of these advanced-risk-type models some guardrails there make sense to me but I think you want to do it in a light-touch way that doesn’t squash innovation,” he added. “We are in a race with China and I think there’s huge upside, obviously, with AI as well. There are a lot of benefits to society along with some risks.”

Thune spoke to reporters after Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) called on the Trump administration to provide a classified briefing to all senators on the risks posed by AI.

“Warning bells are ringing louder than they ever have – and the Trump administration is looking the other way. Well, if they won’t hold themselves accountable, we will. And if Trump does not act, Congress must,” Schumer said in a statement Monday morning.

He said officials need to answer questions about three areas of concern related to AI.

He wants the administration to provide a full accounting of its new framework for testing the most powerful frontier AI models and to detail what it’s doing to prevent AI chips and semiconductor manufacturing equipment from flowing to China.

Schumer said it also needs to explain its plans to defend the United States from increasingly sophisticated AI-enabled cyberattacks.

Trump, meanwhile, has downplayed the dangers and pushed back on calls for more guardrails around AI.

“The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” he wrote on Truth Social. “The Trump Administration has stopped AI ‘people’ from doing bad, or potentially bad, ‘things,’” he wrote on Truth Social Monday. “We already have tremendous CRIMINAL and REGULATORY power over these companies!” There is a SICK conspiracy going on against AI and Data Centers, and the only one that is happy about it is China.”

data.title: Sanders, Bannon to speak at event calling for AI controls
data.description:
Political figures across the aisle, including Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and former Trump White House adviser Steve Bannon, are finding themselves on the same side of a growing fight over artificial intelligence regulations.

Sanders and Bannon are among a handful of political leaders speaking Tuesday at an event advocating controls to keep humans in charge of AI.

The “Pro-Human Assembly,, hosted by the nonprofit Future of Life Institute in D.C., comes as Washington scrambles to address the risks and safety concerns growing around AI.

Concerns were supercharged last week after AI researcher Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic and claimed in an X post that researchers at the frontier labs “believe AI could kill all humans” but push forward anyway.

Coxon warned superintelligence — a hypothetical AI agent that outperforms all of humanity’s cognitive performance — could destroy all of humanity if the technology’s development does not slow down.

Sanders is one of the loudest voices on the left calling for AI regulations. He and Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas) called for a permanent ban on the development and deployment of superintelligence in the wake of recent hackings involving “rogue” models.

Bannon has taken a populist approach to AI, repeatedly warning over the risks of AI and data centers used to power the technology’s development.

Other speakers include Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.), along with Casar, Reps. Chip Roy (R-Texas), Lori Trahan (D-Mass.), Don Beyer (D-Va.) and New York State Assemblyman Alex Bores, who ran a congressional campaign advocating for better oversight of AI model development.

While Democrats and Republicans remain far apart on how to regulate the technology, a growing number of lawmakers agree more needs to be done to ensure AI is developed safely, with the country’s labor workforce in mind.

President Trump, an ally of Bannon, is doubling down on his support for the AI and data center industry. He argued in a post on Truth Social on Monday “only protections needed are a “strong and smart (High IQ!) President,” claiming the government has tremendous criminal and regulatory power” over AI firms already.

data.title: Husted picks up Steak 'n Shake endorsement in Ohio Senate race
data.description:
Steak N’ Shake has thrown its support behind Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) in the toss-up Ohio Senate race —  citing his commitment to the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement as the fast food company touts its alignment with the Trump administration’s health policies. 

“We stand with Husted because he champions the #MAHA movement to clean up the American food supply chain and lower the cost for consumers,” the restaurant wrote on the social media platform X Thursday.

The Indiana based chain, which has highlighted its winning record in political endorsements this primary cycle, took a dig at Husted’s opponent, former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio), for “driving up grocery prices for every Ohio family” through his support of “extreme federal spending.” 

Husted is locked in a tight race against Brown, with Cook Political Report and Decision Desk HQ rating the contest as a “toss up.” Brown served in the Senate for nearly two decades, losing his 2024 reelection bid to now-Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio.)

“Senator Husted is the only candidate fighting to make Ohio healthy, safe, and affordable again. #MAHA,” Steak N’ Shake wrote in response to a video of Husted talking about his food policy stances while standing in front of a Steak N’ Shake stand. 

The burger chain has made a series of moves in recents months in line with the White House’s agenda.

In 2025, Steak N’ Shake committed to removing all seed oils from their restaurants and switched to only serving cane-sugar Coke-a-cola and grade-A Wisconsin sourced butter following priorities set forth by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The company also appointed a “chief MAHA officer” all in an effort to return fast food to its “glory days.” 

Kennedy has sought to reshape nutrition in America since he took over the Department of Health and Human Services, reworking guidelines to follow an “upside down food pyramid” model that prioritizes vegetables, fruits, proteins, dairy and healthy fats at the top and whole grains at the bottom. 

“Today, our government declares war on added sugar, highly processed foods loaded with additives, added sugar and excess salt,” Kennedy said at a January press conference.  

Husted said in the Thursday video that he is fighting for transparency about the ingredients in food so Americans can “make wise, healthy choices about the food you eat.” The Ohio senator has been vocal about his support for food and nutrition reforms. 

“As the executive branch and Congress work together to strengthen a variety of food safety processes, consistent ingredient transparency standards must be part of that conversation,” Husted wrote in a separate post to X in August.

data.title: Vance confirms calls to generals, admirals on US foreign policy
data.description:
Vice President Vance appeared to confirm on Monday a New York Times story that reported he made calls to U.S. military commanders in the Middle East, Asia and Europe to get their assessments on the Iran war. 

“I trust Pete and I trust Dan Caine, but I found that story very weird,” Vance told reporters. “It’s like the vice president calls around to admirals and generals to try to understand America’s foreign policy, of course I do.” 

The Times reported on Thursday that Vance made the calls during the spring and summer after he was directed by President Trump to figure out a way to end the conflict between Washington and Tehran. 

According to the publication, commanders relayed to Vance that they were worried about the supply of Patriot interceptors. The Times also reported that the vice president discussed strategy, objectives, casualty assessments and the Strait of Hormuz. 

Vance reportedly came away from the conversations with concerns after learning how much Tehran was willing to endure in order for their government to survive and relayed this to Trump and those close to the president.  

The vice president, who has voiced opposition to long-term foreign entanglements, was said to have raised concerns about starting a war with Iran. 

Earlier this month he said he would not characterize the U.S. military operation in Iran presently as a “war.” 

“I wouldn’t call it a war. Right now, there is no active shooting. I recognize there have been places where this has flared up,” the vice president told reporters at a press briefing.

data.title: RFK Jr. to headline Children's Health Defense conference in D.C.
data.description:
Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is scheduled to give a keynote address this week at a conference for Children’s Health Defense (CHD), the anti-vaccine advocacy organization he co-founded and led prior to becoming head of the nation’s health agency. 

For the past year Kennedy has worked to distance himself from the efforts of CHD, an organization that questions the safety and efficacy of childhood vaccines and is a leading force of the anti-vaccination movement.   

During his confirmation hearing, Kennedy sought to reassure lawmakers that he would not undermine public confidence in vaccines and maintained he was not anti-vaccine. 

During one memorable exchange, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) displayed images of onesies sold by CHD that read “Unvaxxed, Unafraid” and “No Vax, No Problem.”  

“Are you supportive of these onesies?” Sanders said.  

Kennedy said he had nothing to do with the merchandise and noted he had resigned from the group. 

“I am supportive of vaccines,” Kennedy said at the time. 

Thursday’s conference in Washington, D.C., marks Kennedy’s first appearance at an official CHD conference since he joined the Trump administration, but the group now wields significant political clout. 

Kennedy did not attend the group’s national conference last year.   

Leaders of the organization have been hired in prominent positions at HHS, and views that were once considered fringe — like a false and debunked link between vaccines and autism — have become mainstream in the Trump administration, oftentimes echoed by President Trump himself.  

HHS did not immediately return a request for comment.  

Thursday’s event is touted as a way to “highlight the work of key government officials and individuals who are advocating for transparency, accountability and justice in the area of public health.” 

It comes amid unprecedented efforts by Trump and HHS to roll back childhood vaccines and downplay the severity of vaccine-preventable disease outbreaks, notably measles.  

Aside from Kennedy, the event will feature speeches from lawmakers including Sens. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.) and Rand Paul (R-Ky.), as well as Reps. Paul Gosar (R-Ariz.) and Thomas Massie (R-Ky.). 

The event will also feature Andrew Wakefield, a doctor whose medical license was revoked and who is credited with starting the argument that modern vaccines cause autism. 

Kennedy joined the World Mercury Project, a nonprofit that pressed to remove mercury from vaccines in 2015. He rebranded it as Children’s Health Defense and served as its chairman and top lawyer until 2024, when he stepped down to run for president.  

He earned a six-figure salary at the organization, and millions more helping to sue vaccine makers and challenge state-level vaccine policies. 

The group promotes anti-immunization views as part of its goal to end chronic health conditions in children by “eliminating toxic exposures.”

data.title: 10-year Treasury yield hits 5 percent
data.description:
The 10-year U.S. Treasury bond yield surpassed 5 percent during Monday trading, marking just the second time it has done so in the last 19 years.

The yield on the 10-year Treasury note hit 5.014 percent but has sunk to 4.961 percent as of mid-afternoon Monday, nearly 1 basis point above where it opened.

Monday marked the first time the 10-year bond yield touched 5 percent since October 2023, and just the second time it has done so since July 2007 — before the global financial crisis.

The 10-year bond yield is up 80-plus basis points from the start of this year and more than a full percentage point higher than where it stood at closing time the day before the U.S. and Israel launched the Iran war.

The yield on the 30-year Treasury bond, meanwhile, is down by nearly 2 basis points to less than 5.33 percent as of Monday afternoon. The 30-year bond yield is up by 70 basis points since the day before the Iran conflict started.

Bond yields have risen in the U.S. and other major countries due to persistent inflation amid the Iran war and mounting government debt. The U.S. national debt crossed the $40 trillion threshold last month, with the federal government having paid $1.27 trillion in interest on the debt this fiscal year alone.

President Trump also pledged last week to send every American adult a $5,000 dividend if Republicans maintain control of Congress this November. Trump’s proposal would cost the federal government roughly $1.35 trillion. 

Economist Robin Brooks noted Friday that investors are “aggressively differentiating between high- and low-debt countries,” chalking up the sharp rise in American, French, Japanese, Italian, British and Greek bond yields to a global debt shock.

“Markets are differentiating based on the level of public debt, which they’re only doing because they’re uniquely fixated on this issue,” Brooks, a senior fellow at the Brooks Institute, wrote on Substack. 

Elevated energy costs, as the Iran conflict approaches the seven-month mark, are also contributing to investors’ concerns. West Texas Intermediate crude oil, the North American benchmark, is trading at above $101 per barrel as of Monday afternoon. 

The Trump administration has attempted to tamp down bond yields, so far to no avail. The Treasury Department on Thursday repurchased nearly $5.2 billion worth of 10- to 20-year securities, after increasing its maximum buyback limit from $2 billion to $6 billion.

The Treasury is set to buy back up to $4 billion worth of 7- to 10-year securities on Thursday, according to its operations schedule.

The increase in the 10-year bond yields comes with heavy implications for Americans. The average 30-year mortgage rate, which follows the 10-year bond yield, was 6.76 percent last week — its highest mark since late June 2025.

The week before the U.S. and Israel launched strikes on Iran, the average 30-year mortgage rate was below 6 percent. The average 30-year rate has not topped 7 percent since mid-January of last year.

data.title: Trump weighs in on Flock debate: 'I like them'
data.description:
President Trump on Sunday backed the use of Flock cameras, a controversial surveillance tool.

“Speaking of [artificial intelligence], Flock cameras. You haven’t talked a lot about these Flock cameras. A lot of law enforcement say they really help them. Would you be willing to back that?” a reporter asked Trump on Air Force One.

“No, I sort of like them because of that, because of law enforcement. But some people don’t. They think it’s an infringement,” the president responded, adding later, “I like them.”

Pushback to the AI vehicle surveillance systems operated by Flock Safety has grown on both sides of the aisle.

Flock has a system of license plate readers, video cameras and audio detection devices incorporated into its AI database. That database logs license plate numbers, as well as car features like make, model, color and bumper stickers. Local jurisdictions can share data with other law enforcement agencies, creating a major network that law enforcement can use in crime solving.

Earlier this month, Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), who has been on the president’s bad side in the last few years, unveiled a bill aimed at limiting federal funds used for automated license plate reader cameras (ALPRs) and biometric surveillance cameras.

The legislation, named the Flock-Off Act, would halt any effort to buy, install, maintain, operate or upgrade ALPRs and biometric surveillance cameras for municipalities or local law enforcement.

“Federal taxpayers should not be forced to fund the surveillance state,” Massie said in a post on the social platform X, in which he discussed the bill.

data.title: Sydney Sweeney criticized by women athletes for nude sports prediction market ad
data.description:
Actress Sydney Sweeney is facing criticism from a growing number of female athletes online over a new advertisement for a sports prediction market platform in which she appears wearing little or no clothing.

The advertisement, promoting prediction market platform NoVig, opens with a nude Sweeney asking the camera “think you know sports? Prove it,” while holding two footballs in front of her chest.

In another series of shots, Sweeney sits atop a basketball hoop, crouches in front of a hockey goal keeper’s net and lies on a soccer bench, all with limited or no clothing on.

Several female professional athletes, across a wide array of sports, are expressing outrage at the less than one-minute ad, arguing it objectifies women in sports and is in poor taste.

“idk what Sydney Sweeney was doing but this is what a women in sports looks like,” the American gymnast Gracie Kramer wrote in one post on Instagram, which she captioned “because it really is that deep.”

Skye Nicolson, an Australian professional boxer wrote Sweeney was “giving the ad campaign exactly what they wanted, but honestly these companies need to do better.”

Australian surfer Felicity Palmateer told CNN she found the ad to be “very damaging” for female athletes.

“Just absolute utter disbelief, incredibly disappointing, like, how far you can put women’s sports backwards in the space of a 42-second commercial,” Palmateer said.

Sweeney has not commented publicly on the backlash the ad is receiving, but she reportedly approached NoVig about participating in the ad and the company’s CEO told Front Office Sports she was “great at captivating audiences and being the center of attention.”

The actress has been at the center of controversy in the past, most recently in connection with an advertisement for American Eagle jeans which some critics said smacked of promoting eugenics.

Sweeney told Variety at the time of her work promoting various brands, “I’ve always believed that I’m not here to tell people what to think.”

data.title: Watch live: Jeffries gives remarks as AI safety concerns mount
data.description:
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) will speak with reporters Monday afternoon as calls for guardrails around artificial intelligence (AI) build after industry experts raised red flags around safety of the emerging technology.

Jeffries and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer (N.Y.) have pressed the Trump administration for transparency on how the U.S. will respond to potential threats from AI and what potential regulations could look like. President Trump and GOP leaders have largely brushed off the fears.

His remarks also come as the House faces a shrinking legislative calendar ahead of the November midterms and as Democrats seek to take control of Congress next year.

The press conference is scheduled to begin at 3 p.m. EDT.

Watch the live video above.
